A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FrameFusion by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, GPU runtime and memory measurements, token-similarity analyses, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, model configurations, and experiments on merging strategies, distance metrics, thresholds, and positional embeddings.

M1.justification: Both versions use adjacent-frame cosine similarity, transitive token grouping, averaging into the earliest token, cascaded shallow-layer merging, and subsequent importance-based pruning. The expanded workflow explanation and additional model and image evaluations do not document a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 retains VideoMME, NExT-QA, and VideoNIAH and adds EgoSchema and MVBench. It also evaluates VideoMME with subtitles and introduces image evaluation on MMMU-Pro-standard in Appendix 8.1.6. These additions materially broaden task and input coverage.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares against StreamingLLM, FastV, and dense or reduced-frame models. v2 adds PruMerge to corresponding existing benchmark comparisons, including Table 1 and Figure 7, while explicitly excluding it for MiniCPM-V. It also adds measured non-cascaded merging results where v1 used an empty-cache computational bound.

E3.justification: v2 adds NVILA-2B/8B/15B, Qwen2-VL-7B, and InternVL-2.5-8B configurations and expands the main retrieval frame-count sweep from 64–128 to 8–256. The cascading experiment changes substantially: a non-cascaded baseline with a stated 30% merging rate is compared with cascaded merging at an 84% token budget under matched FLOPs, replacing v1's empty-cache limiting case.

E4.justification: v2 adds downstream accuracy tests for similarity-pair selection, distance-metric comparisons, threshold sensitivity, and a positional-embedding intervention. It broadens merging-layer and merging-order ablations across three benchmarks and implements a direct cascading comparison. The earlier top-k hit-count diagnostic is replaced by average similarity versus merging ratio.

E5.justification: Appendix 8.3.4 newly reports numerical uncertainty for the positional-embedding analysis: 0.0087 ± 0.0010 absolute change and 2.73% ± 0.66% relative change. Existing plots of variance across data items remain. The meaning of the new ± terms and any repeated-run counts are unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, ablation, and efficiency results. For example, Table 10 reports NVILA-15B MMMU-Pro-standard scores of 32.8 for FrameFusion, 36.1 for the dense model, and 30.6 for FastV. Many matched earlier results remain unchanged, including Llava-Video-7B's 30%-budget VideoNIAH scores of 90.0, 48.7, and 87.3; expanded aggregate scores should not be treated as same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: The cosine-similarity and retention definitions in Equations 1–3 and the token-budget and FLOP derivations in Equations 4–6 are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical correction is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contribution, 70% token-reduction claim, and less-than-3% average performance-impact claim remain. The headline end-to-end speedup range increases from 1.6–1.9× in v1's abstract to 1.6–3.6× in v2. This is a limited strengthening of the empirical claim; v1 already reported up to 3.2× in its appendix.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that token content dominates positional embeddings in determining similarity and explains efficiency scaling through attention costs and the relative contribution of other processing overheads. It also discusses performance outside the intended video setting. The existing limitations concerning complex videos and predefined metrics are retained, moving from Section 11 to Section 12.

D1.justification: Appendix 7 adds explicit per-model frame counts and NVILA similarity thresholds, while Section 3.1 specifies that the first 128 VideoMME samples are used. These are additional disclosures, not evidence that retained experiments changed. The code link remains unchanged. One new inconsistency remains: NVILA-8B's threshold is 0.75 in Appendix 7.1.2, but Table 12 marks 0.7 as the default.

R1.justification: New Appendix 11 substantially expands positioning against closely related token-merging methods: EVL-Gen, AIM, and LLaVA-PruMerge. It distinguishes FrameFusion's linear-complexity temporal merging from their quadratic similarity computations and different merging/pruning arrangements. This addresses a related-method family largely missing from v1's importance-pruning-centered discussion.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, similarity analysis, and design rationales are extensively rewritten. Cascading discussion moves from the observation analysis into the design rationale, scalability is integrated into performance reporting, and Appendices 7–8 are reorganized into detailed setup, performance, efficiency, and ablation subsections.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a much broader model-by-benchmark display, Figure 6 gains a layer-placement panel, and Figure 10 adds a detailed workflow. Runtime and memory displays are redesigned, with additional comparison and ablation plots and tables. Existing radar plots, retrieval heatmaps, and video visualizations are largely retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the retained method. PruMerge supplies a relevant merging-based competitor, broader evaluations test generality, and Table 5 replaces v1's empty-cache limiting-case argument with an implemented, FLOP-matched comparison. New metric, threshold, and positional-embedding ablations test important design assumptions. These gains resolve meaningful validation gaps, despite localized reporting problems such as the inconsistent NVILA-8B threshold default.
